title: Switch Statements
summary: Pick one of many cases with switch, group values in a case, switch on conditions, and use fallthrough on purpose.
intro: A long chain of `else if` that compares one value again and again is hard to read. Go's `switch` says the same thing in a flat list of cases, and it never falls into the next case by accident.

steps.title: Switch on a value
steps.body:
`switch value` compares the value with each `case` from top to bottom and runs the first one that matches. A case can list several values separated by commas, and `default` runs when nothing matches.

```go harness
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	day := "sun"
	{{code}}
}
```

```go
switch day {
case "sat", "sun":
	fmt.Println("Weekend")
case "wed":
	fmt.Println("Midweek")
default:
	fmt.Println("Weekday")
}
```

Unlike some other languages, a Go case **does not fall through** into the next one. When its body ends, the whole switch ends, so you never write `break` at the end of a case. Each case value must fit the type of the switch value, so `case "4"` next to an `int` does not compile. Listing the same constant twice in one switch is a compile error too (`duplicate case`).

`default` can sit anywhere in the list, but it only runs after every other case fails, so put it last where readers expect it.

example.title: Weekend or weekday
example.prompt: Print the day, then whether it is a weekend, midweek, or a regular weekday.
example.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	day := "sun"
	fmt.Println("Day:", day)

	switch day {
	case "sat", "sun":
		fmt.Println("Weekend")
	case "wed":
		fmt.Println("Midweek")
	default:
		fmt.Println("Weekday")
	}
}
example.explanation: The switch compares `day` with `"sat"` and `"sun"` first. `"sun"` matches, so it prints `Weekend` and the switch ends right there. The `"wed"` case and `default` are skipped without any `break`. With `day := "mon"`, no case would match and `default` would print `Weekday`.

practice.title: Season of the month
practice.prompt:
Print the month number, then the season it falls in.

1. Keep the line that prints `Month: 4`.
2. Switch on `month`.
3. Print `Winter` for 12, 1, 2, `Spring` for 3, 4, 5, and `Summer` for 6, 7, 8, each group in one case.
4. Print `Autumn` in the `default` case.

Expected output:

```text
Month: 4
Spring
```
practice.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	month := 4
	fmt.Println("Month:", month)

	switch month {
	case 12, 1, 2:
		fmt.Println("Winter")
	case 3, 4, 5:
		fmt.Println("Spring")
	case 6, 7, 8:
		fmt.Println("Summer")
	default:
		fmt.Println("Autumn")
	}
}
hints: List several values in one case with commas: `case 3, 4, 5:`.
You do not need `break`. Each case ends the switch on its own.

steps.title: Switch on conditions
steps.body:
Leave out the value and each case becomes a bool condition. This is the idiomatic Go replacement for a long `if` / `else if` chain.

```go harness
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	score := 85
	{{code}}
}
```

```go
switch {
case score >= 90:
	fmt.Println("A")
case score >= 80:
	fmt.Println("B")
default:
	fmt.Println("F")
}
```

Cases are checked top to bottom and **the first true case wins**, even if later ones are true as well. A score of 95 passes `score >= 80` too, but it never gets there. So order the cases from the strictest to the loosest, just like an else-if chain.

A switch can also start with an init statement, like `if` can. The variable exists only inside the switch:

```go harness
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	n := 10
	{{code}}
}
```

```go
switch r := n % 3; r {
case 0:
	fmt.Println("divides evenly")
default:
	fmt.Println("remainder", r)
}
```

A plain `break` inside a case leaves only the switch, which matters once switches sit inside loops.

example.title: Letter grade and remainder
example.prompt: Turn a score into a letter grade with a switch on conditions, then report a remainder with a switch that has an init statement.
example.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	score := 77
	fmt.Println("Score:", score)

	switch {
	case score >= 90:
		fmt.Println("A")
	case score >= 80:
		fmt.Println("B")
	case score >= 70:
		fmt.Println("C")
	default:
		fmt.Println("F")
	}

	switch r := 10 % 3; r {
	case 0:
		fmt.Println("divides evenly")
	default:
		fmt.Println("remainder", r)
	}
}
example.explanation: The first switch has no value, so Go checks each condition in order. `77 >= 90` and `77 >= 80` are false, `77 >= 70` is true, so it prints `C` and stops. The second switch first runs `r := 10 % 3`, which gives 1, then switches on `r`. No case is `1`, so `default` prints `remainder 1`. Outside that switch, `r` does not exist.

practice.title: Temperature label
practice.prompt:
Label a temperature with a switch on conditions, then report a day offset with a switch that has an init statement.

1. Keep the line that prints `Temp: -2`.
2. Write a switch with no value: below 0 prints `Freezing`, below 15 prints `Cold`, below 25 prints `Mild`, otherwise `Hot`.
3. Write `switch d := 17 % 7; d {` with `case 0:` printing `same day` and a `default` that prints the word `day`, a space, and the value of `d`.

Expected output:

```text
Temp: -2
Freezing
day 3
```
practice.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	temp := -2
	fmt.Println("Temp:", temp)

	switch {
	case temp < 0:
		fmt.Println("Freezing")
	case temp < 15:
		fmt.Println("Cold")
	case temp < 25:
		fmt.Println("Mild")
	default:
		fmt.Println("Hot")
	}

	switch d := 17 % 7; d {
	case 0:
		fmt.Println("same day")
	default:
		fmt.Println("day", d)
	}
}
hints: Start with `case temp < 0:`. The first true case wins, so `temp < 15` only runs for 0 through 14.
In the second switch, `fmt.Println("day", d)` prints `day 3`.

steps.title: fallthrough
steps.body:
Sometimes you *want* one case to continue into the next. Put `fallthrough` as the last statement of a case and Go runs the next case's body too.

```go harness
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	tier := "gold"
	{{code}}
}
```

```go
switch tier {
case "gold":
	fmt.Println("Free shipping")
	fallthrough
case "silver":
	fmt.Println("Priority support")
}
```

Three rules to remember:

- `fallthrough` does **not** check the next case. With `tier` set to `"gold"`, the `"silver"` body runs even though `tier` is not `"silver"`.
- It must be the last statement in its case. You cannot put it inside an `if` or follow it with more code.
- The final case cannot use it, because there is no next case. That is a compile error: `cannot fallthrough final case in switch`.

Use it sparingly. It fits tiers where a higher level includes everything below it. When you only want several values to share one body, list them in one case instead.

example.title: Membership perks
example.prompt: Print every perk a gold member gets, where each tier includes the perks of the tiers below it.
example.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	tier := "gold"
	fmt.Println("Tier:", tier)

	switch tier {
	case "gold":
		fmt.Println("Free shipping")
		fallthrough
	case "silver":
		fmt.Println("Priority support")
		fallthrough
	case "bronze":
		fmt.Println("Member discount")
	}
}
example.output:
Tier: gold
Free shipping
Priority support
Member discount
example.explanation: `tier` matches `"gold"`, which prints `Free shipping` and then falls through. The `"silver"` body runs without its case being checked and falls through again. The `"bronze"` body runs last and has no `fallthrough`, so the switch ends. A silver member would start at the second case and get two perks.

practice.title: Level unlocks
practice.prompt:
Print every item a player has unlocked, where each level also unlocks the items of the levels below it.

1. Keep the line that prints `Level: 2`.
2. Switch on `level` with the cases `3`, `2`, and `1`, in that order.
3. Case 3 prints `Unlocked: Dragon armor`, case 2 prints `Unlocked: Steel sword`, and case 1 prints `Unlocked: Wooden shield`.
4. End cases 3 and 2 with `fallthrough`. Case 1 is last, so it has none.

Expected output:

```text
Level: 2
Unlocked: Steel sword
Unlocked: Wooden shield
```
practice.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	level := 2
	fmt.Println("Level:", level)

	switch level {
	case 3:
		fmt.Println("Unlocked: Dragon armor")
		fallthrough
	case 2:
		fmt.Println("Unlocked: Steel sword")
		fallthrough
	case 1:
		fmt.Println("Unlocked: Wooden shield")
	}
}

tests.output:
Level: 2
Unlocked: Steel sword
Unlocked: Wooden shield

hints: Put `fallthrough` on its own line after the `fmt.Println` in cases 3 and 2.
Level 2 starts at `case 2:`, so the Dragon armor line never prints.

recap:
- `switch v { case a: ... }` runs the first case that equals `v`.
- `case "sat", "sun":` matches any of the listed values.
- `default` runs when no case matches.
- Cases never fall through on their own, so no `break` is needed.
- `switch { case x > 0: }` checks conditions in order, and the first true case wins.
- `switch r := n % 3; r { }` declares a variable that lives only in the switch.
- `fallthrough` runs the next case's body without checking it. It must be last in its case and cannot appear in the final case.
